cards.front: A microscope's {{c1::resolution}} is the smallest gap at which two points still look separate.
cards.back: A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than this limit.
cards.quote: A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than the tool's limit, its resolution (the smallest gap at which two points still look separate).
cards.section: Explore: zoom in and see what appears

cards.front: A micrometer (µm) is one thousandth of a {{c1::millimeter}}.
cards.back: And a nanometer (nm) is one thousandth of a micrometer.
cards.quote: A micrometer (µm) is one thousandth of a millimeter.
cards.section: Explore: zoom in and see what appears

cards.front: Under a microscope, how can a whole cell look clear while its parts do not?
cards.back: The whole cell is larger than the tool's resolution, but its parts are smaller than it, so they blur together. Parts can also be low-contrast, so stains help.
cards.quote: So a whole cell can be clear while its parts are not.
cards.section: Explore: zoom in and see what appears

cards.front: The unaided eye can separate details about 0.1 mm (100 µm) apart. Which can it show clearly: a frog egg (about 1 mm), a human cheek cell (about 50 to 80 µm), a bacterium (about 1 to 2 µm)?
cards.back: Only the frog egg. The cheek cell and the bacterium are smaller than 100 µm, so you need a light microscope to make out their shapes.
cards.why: A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than the tool's limit.
cards.quote: A set of objects sits on the slide: a frog egg (about 1 mm across), a human cheek cell (about 50 to 80 µm)
cards.section: Explore: zoom in and see what appears

cards.front: About how small a detail can an ordinary light microscope separate in biological samples?
cards.back: About 0.2 µm. Special methods can beat this limit.
cards.quote: The 0.2 µm limit belongs to ordinary light microscopes; special methods beat it
cards.section: Explore: zoom in and see what appears

cards.front: About how small a detail can an electron microscope separate in biological samples?
cards.back: About 1 to 2 nm (0.001 to 0.002 µm). The lenses and the delicate sample set this limit.
cards.quote: In practice, the lenses and the delicate sample, not the wavelength, set the 1 to 2 nm limit.
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: Why can an electron microscope separate much finer details than a light microscope?
cards.back: Electrons travel as waves with a much shorter wavelength than visible light, and shorter wavelengths make smaller blurs.
cards.quote: Electrons travel as waves with a much shorter wavelength (the distance from one crest to the next) than visible light, so electrons can separate much finer details
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: Why were ribosomes seen clearly only with electron microscopes?
cards.back: Ribosomes are about 0.02 to 0.03 µm across, far below the light microscope's 0.2 µm limit.
cards.quote: Ribosomes, the cell's protein builders, are about 0.02 to 0.03 µm across, far below the light microscope's limit.
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: An old single-lens microscope separates details 1.35 µm apart. A rod-shaped bacterium is about 1 to 2 µm long. Can the microscope show the bacterium's inner parts? Can it show the bacterium at all?
cards.back: Inner parts: no, they are far smaller than 1.35 µm. At all: yes, as a blurred speck or a rough shape at best.
cards.why: An object near or below the limit can still show up; detecting something is not the same as resolving it.
cards.quote: Detecting something is not the same as resolving it.
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: A student turns an ordinary light microscope to its highest magnification, hoping to see a ribosome (about 0.02 to 0.03 µm) as a shape. What happens and why?
cards.back: The ribosome is still not resolved. More magnification makes the image bigger, but each point is still a smudge, and smudges closer than about 0.2 µm merge.
cards.quote: A tool shows a detail only if the detail is larger than the tool's limit
cards.section: Explore: zoom in and see what appears

cards.front: A {{c1::stain}} is a dye that sticks to some cell parts more than others.
cards.back: It adds contrast.
cards.quote: A stain is a dye that sticks to some cell parts more than others.
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: Many cells are almost clear inside. How do stains help you see parts such as the nucleus?
cards.back: A stain adds contrast, a difference in darkness between a part and its background, so pale parts stand out.
cards.quote: It adds contrast, a difference in darkness between a part and its background.
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: A pale cell part is about 0.05 µm across. A student stains it and looks with an ordinary light microscope. Will its shape be resolved? What tool would work?
cards.back: No. The stain adds contrast, but 0.05 µm is below the 0.2 µm limit. An electron microscope (about 1 to 2 nm limit) could resolve it.
cards.why: Contrast and resolution are separate problems: a stain fixes the first, only a finer tool fixes the second.
cards.quote: Stains made many parts easier to tell apart, and electron microscopes later resolved much finer details inside cells.
cards.section: Explain: seeing smaller things

cards.front: State the six ideas of the cell theory as Virginia lists them.
cards.back: 1) All living organisms are made of cells. 2) Cells are the basic unit of life. 3) All cells arise from pre-existing cells. 4) Metabolism occurs within cells. 5) DNA is passed from cell to cell. 6) All cells have the same basic composition.
cards.quote: All living organisms are composed of cells. Cells are the basic unit of life. All cells arise from pre-existing (already existing) cells.
cards.section: Explain: the six ideas of the cell theory

cards.front: {{c1::Metabolism}} is all the chemical reactions that happen in a living thing.
cards.back: Example: breaking down sugar to release energy for the cell to use.
cards.quote: Metabolism is all the chemical reactions that happen in a living thing
cards.section: Explain: the six ideas of the cell theory

cards.front: In the cell theory, what does "all cells have the same basic composition" mean?
cards.back: Cells are built from the same main kinds of molecules: proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acids. Typical cells also have a membrane, a watery inside and DNA.
cards.quote: "Same basic composition" means that cells are built from the same main kinds of molecules: proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acids
cards.section: Explain: the six ideas of the cell theory

cards.front: A frog egg is about 1 mm across; a bacterium is about 1 to 2 µm long. Does this huge size difference go against the idea that all cells have the same basic composition?
cards.back: No. The idea is about the main kinds of molecules cells are built from, not their size or shape.
cards.quote: The same basic plan does not mean the same size or shape
cards.section: Explain: the six ideas of the cell theory

cards.front: Digestive enzymes break down food in the gut, outside any cell. Does this disprove the idea that metabolism occurs within cells?
cards.back: No. Those enzymes are made by cells, and most of metabolism still happens inside cells.
cards.quote: But those enzymes are made by cells, and most of metabolism happens inside cells.
cards.section: Metabolism outside cells?

cards.front: In science, a theory is a {{c1::well-tested explanation}} of some part of nature, supported by many lines of evidence.
cards.back: Example: the cell theory. It is not a guess.
cards.quote: A well-tested explanation of some part of nature, supported by many lines of evidence
cards.section: Explain: a theory that grew and changed

cards.front: How does a scientific theory differ from a scientific law?
cards.back: A law describes how something behaves under stated conditions. A theory explains why. More evidence does not turn a theory into a law.
cards.quote: A theory explains and a law describes a pattern.
cards.section: Explain: a theory that grew and changed

cards.front: Label each as a hypothesis, a theory or a law: (a) in a closed container the total mass stays the same during a reaction; (b) matter is made of atoms, and reactions rearrange them; (c) all plant tissues are made of cells, not yet tested.
cards.back: (a) Law: it describes. (b) Theory: it explains why. (c) Hypothesis: a testable statement.
cards.quote: The law of conservation of mass says that when a chemical reaction runs in a closed container, the total mass stays the same
cards.section: Explain: a theory that grew and changed

cards.front: Hypothesis: all plant tissues are made of cells. What prediction follows, and how would you test it?
cards.back: If the hypothesis is true, thin slices of other plants should show cells too. Cut and look at thin slices of other plants.
cards.quote: A prediction is what you should observe if a hypothesis is true.
cards.section: Explain: a theory that grew and changed

cards.front: Hooke saw cells in cork. What else did it take to claim cells for all life?
cards.back: Better light microscopes, many comparisons of plant and animal tissues, and a corrected idea about where new cells come from.
cards.quote: Claiming them for all life took better light microscopes, many comparisons and a corrected idea about new cells.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: What did Remak's work in 1852 show about where new cells come from, and what kind of work was it?
cards.back: He published evidence that new cells form by division. It was observing cell division, which tested the earlier fluid idea.
cards.quote: Published evidence that new cells form by division
cards.section: Elaborate: tools and discoveries over time

cards.front: The early cell theory had a wrong idea about how new cells form, and observations of cell division corrected it. Did this weaken the cell theory, and could more evidence ever make it a law?
cards.back: No to both. Revising one part is how a theory grows: evidence can strengthen a theory or lead scientists to revise it, but neither turns it into a law, because a law only describes.
cards.quote: Supporting evidence can strengthen a theory, and contrary evidence can lead scientists to revise it; neither turns a theory into a law.
cards.section: Explain: a theory that grew and changed

cards.front: A Leeuwenhoek microscope magnified 266 times. Ruska's 1933 electron microscope magnified 12,000 times. How many times greater was Ruska's magnification? Round to a whole number.
cards.back: 12,000 ÷ 266 = 45.1, so about 45 times greater.
cards.quote: How many times greater was the magnification of Ruska's 1933 microscope than that of the Leeuwenhoek microscope in the table?
cards.section: Elaborate: tools and discoveries over time

cards.front: A Leeuwenhoek microscope separated details 1.35 µm apart. An ordinary light microscope today separates about 0.2 µm. About how many times finer is the modern limit?
cards.back: 1.35 ÷ 0.2 = 6.75, so about 7 times finer.
cards.quote: An ordinary light microscope today separates about 0.2 µm.
cards.section: Elaborate: tools and discoveries over time

cards.front: A 1937 electron image of a diatom shell showed details 0.13 µm (130 nm) apart. Could an ordinary light microscope have separated those details?
cards.back: No. 0.13 µm is finer than the light microscope's 0.2 µm limit.
cards.quote: the caption gives 130 nm, finer than the light limit
cards.section: Elaborate: tools and discoveries over time

cards.front: Leeuwenhoek saw living single-celled organisms in the 1670s, yet the cell theory came only in the late 1830s and 1850s. What does this gap show about what a theory needs besides tools?
cards.back: Tools were only part of the wait. The theory also needed comparing many plant and animal tissues and testing where new cells come from.
cards.quote: So tools were part of the wait, but not all of it
cards.section: Elaborate: tools and discoveries over time

cards.front: Does slice thickness change how many separate cells you can count in one view of a light microscope? Using onion slices, name the independent and dependent variables, two constants, and how to make the result reliable.
cards.back: Independent: slice thickness. Dependent: cells you can trace all the way around in one view. Constants: same onion, microscope, magnification, light, stain. Reliable: several slides per thickness, several views each, then the mean.
cards.quote: Independent variable: slice thickness, for example very thin, medium and thick.
